To clarify, we have added this sentence at the beginning of mechanistic investigation: “The following studies focused mainly on FOXF1 and FOXK1 as examples of an activator and repressor, respectively, of viral replication and reactivation.” We have also added the names of the FOX proteins on some figure panels with indications regarding whether they are activating or repressive in some places. Regarding the additional experiments, we agree that overexpressed proteins can sometimes be problematic and address this issue below under the relevant major points.
Major points:
- Throughout the manuscript the authors use a ICP0-null HSV-1 virus based on an initial experiment in Figure 1 where they show that both ICP0-null virus and wildtype virus behave similar. However, it would be crucial to repeat some of the key experiments also with a wildtype virus to exclude effects that are due to the absence of ICP0.
Response: We understand the concern. Our rationale for using an ICP0-null virus was that FOX proteins have greater effects on it than on wild-type (WT) virus suggesting that ICP0 interferes with FOX protein functions, making it harder to dissect the mechanisms. We note that in our original submission most of our functional studies were conducted using WT virus (Figs 1-3), and that absence of ICP0 is biologically relevant during latency and the initial stages of reactivation. Nevertheless, we repeated experiments regarding the effects of knocking down CBP/P300 on FOXF1 functions with WT virus and have added the results in Fig. S10B. Moreover, the new ChIP experiments in 293T cells (see below and Fig. 4A) were also conducted using both WT and ICP0-null viruses.
- Along this line, ICP0 is a ubiquitin E3-ligase. Could the authors please show a western blot +/- infection with wt / delta ICP0 virus in cells that have endogenous expression of most of the FOX proteins (e.g. BJ fibroblasts and HepG2). This would show how virus infection affects physiological FOX protein levels and whether ICP0 is able to degrade some of the FOX proteins.
Response: We have done this in 293T cells, which have substantial endogenous expression of most of the FOX proteins we have studied. The results have been added to Fig. S1B. The FOX protein levels were largely unaffected by ICP0. We speculate that ICP0 interference with FOX protein functions may be related to the ability of both ICP0 and FOX proteins to regulate viral chromatin.
- The finding that FOXF1 is supposed to have a different binding motive in the viral genome compared to the host genome is quite unusual. In general, I am critical of ChIP assays in the context of protein overexpression because overexpression often leads to artifacts. Transcription factors possess the ability to bind to DNA and the more transcription factor present, the more binding to DNA. The authors should perform ChIP assays in infected cells (HSV-1 wt / delta ICP0) with endogenous FOXF1 expression with antibody Abcam; ab168383 from Cancer Discov (2018) 8 (2): 234–251. https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-17-0468.
Response: We do not think our data suggest that FOXF1 has different binding motifs in the viral genome relative to the host genome and we did not state that. The two de novo motifs in Fig. 4C look similar and both conform to the RTAAACA consensus sequence. The minor difference may be because the viral genome is too small to allow accurate motif determination. We share the reviewer’s concerns about experiments using overexpression. Our original thought was to study this in neuronal cells where FOXF1 is poorly expressed so we used overexpression to mimic the condition where FOXF1 expression is induced due to stresses. We thank the reviewer for providing information about the antibody. We have used the antibody for ChIP-qPCR in 293T cells and have demonstrated FOXF1 association with all the viral sites as well as two host sites tested. Two of the viral sites tested (in UL22 and UL50 genes) conform to the motifs in Fig. 4C and two of the viral sites (in ICP8 and ICP27 promoters) do not conform to it supporting our finding that FOXF1 associates with viral DNA in both sequence-specific and nonspecific manners. These new data are in Fig. 4A. This indeed strengthens the argument that FOXF1 can associate with viral DNA broadly in physiological conditions.
- In addition, the authors must include a suitable transfection control protein in their ChIP-seq. assay and ChIP assays in Figure 4 and 6. Desirable would be to use another FOX transcription factor from Figure 1 that did not affect HSV-1 replication like FOXO1.
Response: Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we used FOXP1 (for which we found a good commercially available antibody) as a transfection control for the added experiment of FOXF1 ChIP in 293T cells (Fig. 4A). However, we detected FOXP1 association with both the host and viral DNA sites (FOXF1 association is still higher than FOXP1, but they are both much higher than the IgG negative control). This is not surprising because FOX proteins have similar binding motifs. This raises the interesting possibility that FOX proteins generally associate with the viral genome but such association is insufficient to confer regulation of viral genes.
With regard to Fig. 6I, it was performed using a cell line with inducible FOXF1 expression, not by transfection. Nevertheless, we added an experiment which examined the effects of transfected FOXF1 on H3K27ac/H3, where both transfected FOXP1 and the empty vector were used as negative controls (Fig. 5D, right panel). The results recapitulated the results using inducible cell lines (Fig. 5C) and also showed similar H3K27ac/H3 values between FOXP1 and the empty vector-transfected cells suggesting that the results in Fig. 6I from inducible cell lines should be valid.
- The authors should also show selected regions from the host genome in order to compare FOXF1 binding to the human genome upon FOXF1 overexpression with more physiological settings e.g. from Cancer Discov (2018) 8 (2): 234–251. A list with all binding sites in the host and viral genomes in the supplement would also help.
Response: The positions of viral and host peaks and their corresponding genes are listed in Supplementary Data File 1. For host sites, since they are too numerous, we selected the top 1000. Among them are many binding sites in the mouse genome reported previously (Data source: Cistrome Data Browser, GSM2062274), such as Sfi1, Bcl10, Mpzl1, Fos, Tex14, Ablim1, Fcho2, Ints3, Pitpnc1, Ncor2, etc. The experiments in the recommended Cancer Discov article used human cells, but we used mouse cells, so the sequences are not directly comparable. Nevertheless, we detected peaks on Etv1 and Gpr20 genes, which were identified as FOXF1 targets also in the published study.
- For Figure 5C, does FOXF1 expression also induce changes in Histone H3 / Histone modifications at binding sites in cellular chromatin?
Response: We analyzed sites in cellular Fos and Etv1 genes, which are high-ranking host sites in our ChIP-seq data. We see that on the Etv1 site, both H3K18ac/H3 and H3K27ac/H3 ratios were increased by induced FOXF1 expression, with the same trend observed with the Fos site. However, H3 and H3K9me3/H3 on these sites were not reduced like the viral sites. We conclude that inducing histone acetylation may be a FOXF1 function applicable to both viral and host genes. The added data are in Fig. S6B.
- The authors show dispersal of PML-nuclear bodies by FOXF1. That would mean that cell lines like HeLa, 293T and BJ fibroblasts that express FOXF1 (Fig. 2A) should not have PML bodies, which is obviously not the case. In addition, ICP0 is highly efficient in degrading PML-nuclear bodies. This would mean that disruption of PML bodies by FOXF1 has no physiological relevance in the context of wildtype infections because it is anyway rapidly degraded upon infection. Could the authors please comment.
Response: The reviewer’s argument about the PML-NB makes sense, but the argument about ICP0 makes sense only with regard to acute infection. During latent infection as well as the initial stage of reactivation, there is little or no ICP0 expression, so FOXF1 can regulate PML bodies in these stages of infection. Regardless, we admit that it is possible that we introduced FOXF1 to levels that were artificially high. Therefore, we downplay this part by deleting the corresponding supplemental data. We have kept the panel in the main text because we still think FOXF1 dispersal of PML bodies is an interesting phenomenon that deserves revealing, and it may be physiologically relevant under stress conditions where certain Fox genes are strongly induced according to our data in Fig. 2. We also added the following sentence as a caution in the text: “Although these results may be an artifact of FOXF1 overexpression, we note that…”.
- Minor point:
The study would benefit from IF experiments analyzing the presence of FOX proteins in viral replication compartments e.g. by co-staining with ICP8.
Response: This has been done and we see partial colocalization. The additional results are in Fig. S4A. We used an ICP4 antibody to stain replication compartments, which in our hands works well.
- In some experiments (e.g. in Figures 4 F,H,I,J) the authors used a low MOI of 0.2 and virus was titrated after 48h. Would the effect be the same with higher MOI of 1 after 24h?
Response: We understand the reason to check effects at higher MOIs and shorter times. We did the experiment using the W122A mutants as a representative (see below). The result is the same as MOI of 0.2 and 48 h. We believe the other mutants also behave similar between the two conditions. We do not see a need to put this in the manuscript given the already crowded figures.

Response: We agree that it would be best to have the ChIP and ATAC-seq done on latently infected neurons. However, this is technically challenging for us. Neurons are trivial to handle and transgene expression in them is often not very high. Therefore, we used models in primary neurons or iPSC-derived neurons mainly for functional validation, and used the Neuro-2a cell line for mechanistic investigation after showing that effects of FOX proteins in Neuro-2a cells and neurons were consistent.

Response: We apologize for the negligence. In fact, siRNAs all have the two nucleotide 3’ overhangs. They have been added to Table S1. We also added Western blot validation of MAX siRNAs (Fig. S11A).
The authors indicate that BoHV-1 inefficiently infects N2A neurons, and use an MOI of 5 MDBK units. Could the authors provide a relative MOI for N2A cells based on TCID50 assays and immunofluorescence?

Surprisingly, the titers of the BoHV-1 stock, which was determined to be 3.6 x 108 PFU/ml in bovine MDBK cells were determined to be 4 x 108 TCID50/ml in Neuro-2a cells indicating that Neuro-2a cells are equally susceptible to BoHV-1. Therefore, we revised that part like this: “TCID assays of BoHV-1 stocks in Neuro-2a cells showed slow 50 development of cytopathic effects but TCID titers similar to PFU titers in bovine kidney 50 MDBK cells indicating efficient entry but inefficient replication. Regardless, sufficient BoHV- 1 yields were obtained in Neuro-2a cells by using a high MOI (Fig. S2C)”

According to the locations of the RTAAACA motif on the viral genome (green) in Fig. 4B, all RTAAACA sequences have peaks associated with them. Originally, we focused only on the few highest peaks and missed this important point. The text has been revised: “all RTAAACA sequences in the viral genome have peaks associated with them. Without a marker for infection, it is difficult to claim that the cells in Fig. S6B are both infected and transfected. There is only one cell, in the FOXF1+WT HSV panel at the bottom right, that shows a dispersal of DAPI signal due to viral replication compartments.
Response: The reviewer’s question is very reasonable. This experiment lacks a marker for infection. However, considering Reviewer 1’s concern, we have decided to downplay this part about the PML body and delete this supplemental figure.

Response: Revised as suggested.

Response: The description has been added: “we first utilized previously constructed a recombinant HSV-1 expressing FOXC1 (HSV1FOXC1) and, as controls, two viruses, each of which expresses an inactive FOXC1 mutant with both N-terminal and C-terminal activating domains of FOXC1 deleted (HSV1FOXC1delAD and HSV1FOXC1delADb)”.

Response: Yes. We mean PLO. But on second thought, there is no need to add an abbreviation here, so we deleted the abbreviation.
Line 649: place a space in the middle of "pH8.0" for consistency
Response: Revised as suggested.
The supplemental figures do not need "supplemental data" in the title
Response: Revised as suggested.
The ChIP and ATAC-seq are already publicly available, but I was unable to locate the proteomics data with the given accession number
Response: We apologize for the problem. There were some technical issues, which have been resolved. We have confirmed that the data is accessible by using the accession number PXD059232 in https://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org.

The authors should provide more detailed information on how the proteomic data were processed, including steps such as the handling of missing values, removal of potential contaminants, normalization procedures, and any filtering criteria applied. Response: We have rewritten the Methods section about mass spectrometry data analysis including these details: “The acquired .RAW files were loaded into DIA-NN (version 1.9) for spectra-library-free search against the all SwissProt protein sequences of mouse and HSV-1 proteomes. Trypsin with up to two missed cleavages was set. Carbamidomethyl (C) was set as fixed modification. Oxidation (M) and acetyl (protein N-term) were set as variable modifications. Mass tolerance of 7 ppm and 15 ppm were set for MS and MS2 spectra, respectively. Protein level 1% FDR was set to filter the result. Potential contaminant proteins were identified by DIA-NN build-in database and were removed from subsequent analysis. For quantitative analysis, missing values were filled with a MS intensity of 1000 (noise level), and all intensity values were log2-transformed. Proteins enriched in the TurboID samples were then selected using a t-test (P value < 0.05) in Excel and required a fold-change of at least 2 (corresponding to an average intergroup difference of ≥ 1 on the log2 scale).”
However, we did not perform normalization in this case. For whole proteome experiments, where it is assumed that the expression levels of the vast majority of proteins remain unchanged, we usually perform median or global normalization. However, for experiments like proximity labeling or co-IP-MS, the differences of identified proteins and their intensities among different groups are very significant, so in such cases, we generally do not force global normalization，which can artificially reduce the inter-group differences, leading to false negative results.
3. The authors may consider validating the nuclear localisation of the TurboID-tagged FOX constructs using IF to confirm their proper subcellular distribution, and include these data in Fig. S8.
Response: We have done this experiment and the data are now included in Fig. S8B. Basically, all TurboID-FOX fusion proteins are in the nucleus but unfused TurboID is in the cytoplasm.
4. Fig. 6: It would be helpful to include a Venn diagram in to highlight the 11 proteins enriched by more than 2 log2 in all pairwise comparisons. This addition would improve the overall flow of the figure and help readers more easily understand the rationale behind validating the interaction with CBP in panels C–E, as well as the selection of genes shown in panel F for silencing experiments.
Response: The Venn diagram was already in Fig. S8C in the original manuscript. Now we have moved it to Fig. 6B and moved the original Fig. 6B (about KEGG analysis) to Fig. S8D.
5. Fig. 7A: Would MAX, KIN, GTF2A1, SIN3A, and ARID4B still be considered hits if a more stringent cut-off of log₂ fold-change > 2 were applied, as was done for the FOXF1 dataset? This may be particularly relevant given that MAX and SIN3A were not successfully validated in the co-IP assays, which—beyond the possibility of a temporal or indirect interaction, as the authors suggest—could also indicate that the interactions are generally weaker. Along these lines, were the authors able to validate, via co-IP, the interaction between FOXK1 and any other protein that showed a similar level of enrichment as MAX or SIN3A? Generally, increasing the amount of protein input in co-IP assays can improve the likelihood of successful detection, which might be worth considering if validation has been challenging.
Response: Applying a cut-off of log₂ fold-change > 2 gave rise to MAX, KIN and GTF2A1 only. We decided to use log₂ fold-change > 1 because we think SIN3A is a very interesting candidate and its interaction with FOXK1 has been previously reported. We did not validate the interaction between FOXK1 and other proteins because they do not show effects on viral replication. To try to address this comment, we tried more experiments to validate the interaction between FOXK1 and SIN3A given that previous studies reported FOXK1-SIN3A interactions in yeast two-hybrid and co-immunoprecipitation assays. We have attempted increasing the input protein quantity in 293T (Fig A) and Neuro-2a cells (Fig B), but still could not detect the interactions. We also tried leaving out benzonase (we’ve always added it for detecting DNA-independent interactions), but the result was also negative (Fig C). Therefore, we believe that these interactions were transient, indirect or weak despite that close proximity. We do not see the need to include these additional negative data, but we have revised that sentence: “It is possible that these protein-protein interactions are transient, weak and/or indirect, so that they did not persist during our co-immunoprecipitation assay.”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors addressed almost all points raised by the reviewers. For my part, concerning the overexpression of FOX proteins and binding of FOX proteins to the host/virus genome the authors show additional controls and experiments with endogenous protein levels that confirmed previous experiments and strengthen their findings. I still don't understand the exact mechanism given different binding patterns in the host and viral genome and differences in the chromatin between viral and host genomes, e.g. that differences in chromatin accessibility are independent on FOX binding sites. However, the authors convincingly show FOXF1 dependent recruitment of the histone acetyltransferase p300/CBP to the viral genome, resulting in changes in chromatin accessibility and histone acetylation and conversely that the repressive effect of FOXK1 is also dependent on histone acetylation. In my opinion, the quality of the manuscript improved and I think that the paper is well-suited for publication in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have performed a comprehensive revision of their manuscript, which investigates how FOX transcription factors (specifically FOXF1 and FOXK1) act as epigenetic regulators of the HSV-1 lytic-latent cycle. The revision has greatly strengthened the manuscript, particularly in its transition from broad observations across the FOX family to a more focused exploration of specific activator and repressor proteins. The addition of experiments using wild-type (WT) virus and endogenous protein assays significantly strengthens the biological relevance of the findings, such as ChIP-Seq of endogenous FOXF1 in 293T cells.
The authors have addressed my previous concerns with new data, data accessibility, figure/table editing, and text revisions. The study provides a significant advancement in our understanding of how the host epigenetic machinery is leveraged to control the herpesvirus life cycle. I have no additional comments or concerns except to point out that in the methods for immunofluorescence, the new text should have a space between "antibody" and the parentheses.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: All of my comments have been addressed and I believe the manuscript is now ready for publication.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The lytic-latent balance is a major viral persistence strategy and obstacle to curing viral diseases, yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. Following lytic infection in non-neuronal cells, herpes simplex virus (HSV) establishes latency specifically in neurons and is reactivated by stresses. Here we identify forkhead box (FOX) transcription factors that can strongly activate or repress replication of HSV-1 and other alphaherpesviruses, and show that neurons express activating Fox (e.g., Foxf) genes poorly but repressive Fox (Foxk) genes abundantly while non-neuronal or stressed neuronal cells exhibit higher expression of activating Fox genes. Remarkably, knockdown of Foxk1 or overexpression of activating Fox genes induces reactivation from latency in male mouse neuronal culture and in vivo. Of note, FOX proteins bind the viral genome globally and non sequence-specifically and interact with epigenetic cofactors for gene regulation. FOXF1 interacts with CBP and P300 to acetylate and open viral chromatin. FOXK1 works with SIN3A, a cofactor of histone deacetylation, and MAX to suppress HSV-1 and antagonize activating FOX proteins. Therefore, the viral lytic-latent balance is controlled by the relative abundance of counteracting host transcription factors that recruit different epigenetic regulators to the viral genome.

---

## Introduction

Switching between productive (lytic) and latent infections is a common strategy of many viruses to persist in hosts, and a major obstacle for curing viral diseases. Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) is an ubiquitous pathogen that causes numerous human diseases. During lytic infection, after entry of the viral DNA genome into the nucleus, viral genes are expressed in the order of immediate-early (IE), early (E) and late (L) genes leading to abundant production of viral genomes and particles. In vivo, after lytic infection in non-neuronal cells of peripheral tissues, HSV establishes latent infection particularly in sensory neurons where essentially all viral genes except the locus encoding the latency-associated transcript (LAT) are silenced and production of new viral genomes and particles ceases. Sporadically, certain stresses can reactate the latent virus to resume the lytic program. HSV has evolved to strike a delicate balance between the two infection programs for optimal prevalence: while lytic infection is essential for viral propagation, toomuch of it may cause death or evoke immune responses strong enough to clear the virus; while latency facilitates immune evasion, too deep latency may preclude spread.

Because essentially all HSV-1 proteins are used for replication, the virus relies heavily on host factors for latency, among which epigenetic factors play an important role. During latency in vivo, the HSV-1 genome associates with histones with high levels of heterochromatin modifications such as H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, and inhibitors of the relevant histone demethylases can decrease reactivation. PI3K, mTOR and DNA damage response pathways, as well as the intrinsic and innate immunity mediated by PML nuclear body (PML-NB) components and type I interferons are also implicated in latency. Notably, it is becoming clearer that intrinsic features of neurons favor HSV latency. The viral activator VP16 was shown to dissociate from the viral capsid in the neuronal axons so that it cannot efficiently reach the nucleus to activate gene transcription. We showed that neuron-specific host microRNAs miR-138 and miR-9 repress the expression of multiple viral and host activators of HSV gene expression. Regarding the mechanisms of reactivation, it has been hypothesized that stress-related JNK and DLK pathways lead to an initial step of viral gene de-repression before full reactivation. The glucocorticoid receptor could activate lytic gene promoters in transfection assays, and its mutation reduced reactivation in female mice. Taken together, despite the previous work revealing upstream pathways involved, little is known about what directly acts on the viral genome to enable latency specifically in neurons and reactivation under stresses.

Our previous studies showed that FOXC1, a target of miR-138, promotes HSV-1 neuronal replication. FOXC1 belongs to the forkhead box (FOX) transcription factor family, which comprises 50 genes classified into 19 subfamilies in humans. FOX proteins share a conserved winged helix forkhead DNA binding domain (DBD). They play pivotal roles in various biological processes including development, metabolism and oncogenesis. Notably, the FOXA subfamily members are known as pioneer factors, which are transcription factors capable of accessing and then opening condensed chromatin. However, the roles of FOX proteins in viral infection remain largely unexplored. For herpesviruses, we are aware of only a few related reports, which were about regulation of human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) or Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) by FOXO or FOXK proteins. Aside from our own studies regarding FOXC1, we are unaware of any reports on roles of FOX proteins in HSV infection.

In this work, we identified multiple FOX proteins that can strongly activate or repress neuronal replication of HSV-1 and other alpha-herpesviruses. These proteins are expressed in ways that correlate with the viral phenotypes of latency or lytic replication, and perturbation of their expression profoundly impacts the lytic-latent balance in neuronal culture and in vivo. Mechanistically, the FOX proteins widely associate with viral DNA and cooperate with epigenetic regulators to modulate viral chromatin. These results lead to a new model about how the viral lytic-latent balance is controlled.

---

## Results

Identification of FOX proteins that can strongly activate or repress HSV-1 neuronal replication
To identify FOX family proteins that can regulate HSV-1 infection, we first selected one member from each subfamily and transfected their human genes before infecting mouse neuroblastoma Neuro-2a cells (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a). If a Fox gene from a subfamily had an effect, other members of the subfamily were also tested. In case the viral E3 ubiquitin ligase ICP0 interfered with these functions, both wild-type (WT) strain KOS and its ICP0-null mutant (7134 virus) were used. Proteins with significant impacts on both viruses at a low multiplicity of infection (MOI) were selected. Thus, FOXA1, A2, A3, C1, C2, E1, F1 and F2 that could substantially increase viral yields are designated activating FOX proteins, and FOXK1 and K2 with opposite effects are designated repressive FOX proteins (Fig. 1a). The effects were generally greater on ICP0-null than WT HSV-1 suggesting that ICP0 indeed interfered with FOX protein effects. To test whether this could be due to degradation of FOX proteins induced by ICP0, we examined FOXA1, C1, F1 and K1 expression in human embryonic kidney 293T cells infected with either WT or ICP0-null virus. Expression of these FOX proteins was similar following infection by the two viruses, with the possible exception of less FOXK1 expression in WT infected cells (Supplementary Fig. 1b), implying that instead of targeting FOX proteins for degradation, ICP0 might interfere with downstream steps regulated by the FOX proteins. To avoid such confounding interference, some mechanistic studies described below used ICP0-null virus.

For representative activating FOXF1 and repressive FOXK1, their impacts were confirmed by growth curves (Fig. 1b) and by using Neuro-2a cells stably transduced with these genes for doxycycline (DOX)-inducible expression (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 1a). Even at a high MOI, FOXK1 could also suppress both viruses, although FOXF1 could stimulate ICP0-null but not WT HSV-1 (Fig. 1d). Mouse FOXF1 and FOXK1 had the same effects as their human counterparts (Supplementary Fig. 1a, c), providing support for using mice or mouse cells to study the human proteins. The natural sites of HSV-1 infection and latency are human sensory neurons. Therefore, we employed human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)-derived sensory neurons (iNeurons), and found that lentivirus transduced FOXA1, C1, E1 and F1 all substantially increased WT HSV-1 yields while FOXK1 decreased them (Fig. 1e). However, in 293T cells, transfected FOXF1 had no effect on either virus although FOXK1 decreased yields of both viruses (Fig. 1f). In human foreskin fibroblast (HFF) cells, transduced FOXF1 increased yields of ICP0-null but not WT virus while FOXK1 had no significant effect on either virus (Fig. 1g). Therefore, the effects of FOX proteins are cell-type specific but conserved in human and mouse neuronal cells.

FOX proteins can also regulate other alphaherpesviruses
To test whether similar neurotropic viruses are regulated by FOX proteins, transfection-infection experiments were conducted for some other alphaherpesviruses, including HSV-2, pseudorabies virus (PRV), and bovine herpesvirus 1 (BoHV-1) (Supplementary Fig. 2a–c). HSV-2 and PRV, but not BoHV-1, efficiently infected Neuro-2a cells. TCID50 assays of BoHV-1 stocks in Neuro-2a cells showed slow development of cytopathic effects but TCID50 titers similar to PFU titers in bovine kidney MDBK cells indicating efficient entry but inefficient replication. Regardless, sufficient BoHV-1 yields were obtained in Neuro-2a cells by using a high MOI (Supplementary Fig. 2c). For all three viruses, FOXF1 or K1 significantly increased or decreased viral yields, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2a–c). We found that varicella-zoster virus (VZV) cannot infect Neuro-2a cells, but its gene expression could be detected after the genome was transfected. Co-transfecting FOXF1 with the VZV genome significantly increased IE61 (homolog of HSV ICP0) and IE62 (homolog of HSV ICP4) mRNA levels, while FOXK1 decreased IE61 but not IE62 mRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 2d). Thus, the role of FOX proteins in regulating neuronal viral replication maybe conserved in at least some alphaherpesviruses.

Fox gene expression profiles in neurons favor suppression of HSV-1
To learn about the expression patterns of Fox genes, we turned to RNA-seq resources including reported data for Neuro-2a, 293T and Vero cells (Gene Expression Omnibus GSE182742), and the database for some other cell lines (https://www.proteinatlas.org/), as well as RNA-seq data that we generated for mock-infected human iNeurons (Fig. 2a). Normalized transcript levels showed that Foxk1 and k2 are expressed abundantly in all cell lines examined whereas the activating Fox genes display differences between neuronal and non-neuronal cells. All the non-neuronal cells expressed multiple activating Fox genes abundantly with particular high expression of one or more of them. However, the neurons and neuronal cell lines all showed almost undetectable Foxe or Foxf mRNAs, and low to medium levels of certain Foxa or Foxc mRNAs. In particular, all the activating Fox genes were weakly expressed in iNeurons. Therefore, neuronal cells generally express activating Fox genes poorly but repressive Fox genes abundantly, which, based on our results above, should favor suppression of HSV-1.

Acute infection and stresses upregulate certain activating Fox genes
Next, we examined whether Fox gene expression is altered during infection or other stresses. In our RNA-seq data from HSV-1 infected iNeurons, although each experiment lacked replicates, two experiments, one with infection at MOI 1 and one at MOI 10, both hinted at upregulation of Foxc1 (Supplementary Fig. 3a). We then infected mouse trigeminal ganglia (TG) in vivo following corneal inoculation with WT HSV-1. Relative to mock-infection, acute infection upregulated Foxa3, c1 and f1, and possibly Foxa1 (P = 0.056) at 3 days post-infection (dpi) without affecting repressive Fox genes (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 3b). Latent infection upregulated both activating (Foxc2, f1 and f2) and repressive (Foxk1 and k2) Fox genes at 30 dpi (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 3c). Explant of latently infected TG, which mimics neural damage that causes HSV-1 recurrences clinically, can trigger reactivation. Relative to TG without explant, explant for only 6 h caused upregulation of Foxa2, Foxa3 and Foxf1 by ~2-, 100- and 6.6-fold, respectively, although these changes were independent of infection since mock-infected TG were affected similarly by explant (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 3c). Hyperthermia can trigger reactivation too at least in mice. In Neuro-2a cells treated with hyperthermia (43 °C for 1 h), Foxa3, c2 and f1 were upregulated by 12-, 6- and 3-fold, respectively (Fig. 2d). Neither explant nor hyperthermia affected Foxk1 or k2 mRNA levels. Thus, acute infection and reactivation-related stresses upregulate certain activating Fox genes without affecting repressive Fox genes.

FOXK1 suppresses lytic replication and is important for HSV-1 latency
Given their abundance, we examined the role of endogenous FOXK proteins. Knockout (KO) of FOXK1 in Neuro-2a cells increased ICP0-null virus yields, which were reduced again by transfected FOXK1 (Fig. 3a). In the FOXK1 KO cells, siRNAs that effectively knocked down FOXK2 (Supplementary Table 1) increased viral yields further (Fig. 3b). We then employed a mouse primary TG neuron model of latency and reactivation, which usually relies on chemical triggers to induce reactivation. Considering possible functional redundancy between FOXK1 and K2, we attempted dual knockdown. We selected one shRNA for FOXK1 and one for FOXK2 that effectively knocked down the respective proteins (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Remarkably, even without chemical triggers, dual knockdown of FOXK1 and K2 caused reactivation from latency in 50% of the wells, significantly higher than the 14% of control wells reactivated (Fig. 3c).

To examine the role of FOXK1 in vivo, we generated FOXK1f/f mice with LoxP sites flanking the Foxk1 gene and crossed them with Advillin-Cre (AvilCre+/−) mice which express Cre specifically in sensory neurons. The resulting FOXK1-conditional knockout (cKO) (AvilCre+/−Foxk1f/f) mice expressed less FOXK1 in TG than the control AvilCre−/−Foxk1f/f mice (Fig. 3d). After corneal inoculation, viral titers in tear films from FOXK1-cKO mice were not different from those in control mice at 1 and 3 dpi (Fig. 3e) but were significantly higher in TG at 3 dpi (Fig. 3f) consistent with FOXK1 specifically repressing HSV-1 replication in sensory neurons. Accordingly, viral genome levels in FOXK1-cKO mice were also higher at 3 and 5 dpi (Fig. 3g). However, latent viral genome levels at 30 dpi were essentially identical between FOXK1-cKO and control mice (Fig. 3h). Nevertheless, following explant, the virus reactivated from latently infected TG of FOXK1-cKO mice faster than those of control mice (Fig. 3i). Therefore, FOXK1 not only suppresses acute viral replication to expedite latency establishment, but is also important for latency maintenance.

Activating Fox proteins are sufficient to stimulate reactivation from latency
To investigate the effects of activating Fox proteins on latency, we first utilized previously constructed a recombinant HSV-1 expressing FOXC1 (HSV1FOXC1) and, as controls, two viruses, each of which expresses an inactive FOXC1 mutant with both N-terminal and C-terminal activating domains of FOXC1 deleted (HSV1FOXC1delAD and HSV1FOXC1delADb). In our previous study, HSV1FOXC1 exhibited increased acute titers and similar latent viral loads in mouse TG relative to the control viruses, but reactivation was not tested. Here we found that after corneal inoculation and latent infection of mice in vivo, HSV1FOXC1 reactivated significantly faster than both control viruses during explant of the latently infected TG (Fig. 3j). We then employed the mouse neuronal model of HSV-1 latency mentioned above, and found that even without chemical inducers, transduced Foxa1, c1, e1 and f1 could all lead to 40–60% of wells reactivated, significantly higher than the <10% of control wells reactivated (Fig. 3k). Therefore, increased expression of activating Fox genes is sufficient to trigger reactivation from latency.

Widespread occupancy of FOXF1 on the HSV-1 genome
To understand how FOX proteins regulate HSV-1 infection, we first asked whether these proteins associate with viral DNA. The following studies focused mainly on FOXF1 and FOXK1 as examples of an activator and repressor, respectively, of viral replication and reactivation. We first performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR using an anti-FOXF1 antibody to analyze DNA association in HSV-1-infected 293T cells, where endogenous FOXF1 is abundant (Fig. 4a). As positive controls, regions in host Gpr20 and Kit gene enhancers, which are known to associate with FOXF1, were significantly enriched in DNA precipitated by the FOXF1 antibody relative to the negative control IgG. For both WT and ICP0-null viruses, FOXF1 associated strongly not only with regions within viral UL22 and UL50 genes that contain the DNA motif for FOXF1 association, but also with ICP8 and ICP27 promoters that contain no such sequence. An antibody against FOXP1, which does not regulate HSV-1 (Fig. 1a), also precipitated DNA enriched with these regions simply implying that DNA association is insufficient to confer gene regulation. Additionally, we observed that some FOXC1 co-localized with viral replication compartments (Supplementary Fig. 4a), also consistent with association of FOX proteins with viral DNA.

To investigate this in neuronal cells, where FOXF1 is poorly expressed, we conducted ChIP-seq by pulling down transfected FOXF1 in Neuro-2a cells infected with ICP0-null virus. The positions of viral and host peaks and their corresponding genes are listed in Supplementary Data 1. Validating the results, many host peaks are positioned on FOXF1 target sites reported previously in a database (Datasource: Cistrome Data Browser, GSM2062274) and a published report, including those within Etv1, Gpr20, Fos, Sfi1 and Bcl10 genes. Regarding the viral genome, the data reveal widespread occupancies of FOXF1 on numerous sites that were highly consistent between two biological replicates (Fig. 4b). The fraction of viral reads in total reads was 16-fold higher in the immunoprecipitated samples than input samples further indicating high enrichment of viral DNA associated with FOXF1 (Fig. 4c). The viral peaks showed little or no enrichment around transcription start sites (TSS), contrasting with clear enrichment of host peaks at TSS (Supplementary Fig. 4b) indicating differential occupancy patterns between viral and host DNA. Motif search identified the known DNA motif for FOXF1 as well as some de novo motifs that all conform to a RTAAACA sequence (R = purine) (Fig. 4c). Indeed, all RTAAACA sequences in the viral genome have peaks associated with them. However, many other viral sequences also show peaks despite lacking this consensus sequence, and ChIP-qPCR results showed that besides associating with the sites containing RTAAACA (motif+ sites) in the UL2, UL22 and UL55 genes, FOXF1 also associated with the ICP27 and ICP8 promoters lacking RTAAACA (motif− sites) (Fig. 4d). Thus, FOXF1 extensively associates with the HSV-1 genome in both sequence-specific and non sequence-specific (non-specific) manners.

Non-specific DNA interactions are crucial for HSV-1 regulation by FOX proteins
We also performed ChIP-qPCR for repressive FOXK1 and found robust association with the same set of viral sites as for FOXF1 above (Fig. 4e). FOX proteins comprise well-defined DBDs as well as other domains that are well-defined for FOXA and C proteins but less so for FOXE, F or K proteins (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). By using plasmids expressing truncated proteins (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d), we found that HSV-1 stimulation by FOXF1 required its DBD and the region between aa200–300 (Supplementary Fig. 5e) while efficient suppression by FOXK1 required its DBD, the C-terminus and possibly N-terminus (Supplementary Fig. 5f) suggesting that the DBDs were necessary but insufficient for virus regulation. We further constructed plasmids expressing proteins with the DBD of FOXC1 replaced with that of FOXA1, E1, F1 or K1 (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d). Remarkably, the chimeric proteins, even including the one with the DBD of repressive FOXK1, could all strongly stimulate viral replication (Fig. 4f) indicating that DBDs of different FOX proteins function similarly but are insufficient to determine activation or repression. Based on a crystal structure, the FOXC2 DBD contacts DNA mainly through an asparagine-histidine (NH) site that interacts with DNA bases, and arginine-arginine (RR) and serine-tryptophan (SW) sites that interact with DNA backbones (Fig. 4g). Surprisingly, mutating the corresponding NH site in FOXC1 had no effect on virus stimulation, mutating the RR site had partial effects, while mutating both residues or just the tryptophan of the SW site eliminated stimulation (Supplementary Fig. 5g). Similar mutagenesis studies of FOXF1 showed that among the three sites, only the corresponding tryptophan in the HW site (the serine in the FOXC SW site becomes histidine in FOXF1) is essential for stimulation (Fig. 4h). Moreover, substitution of this tryptophan eliminated virus stimulation by FOXA2 and E1 and attenuated suppression by FOXK1 (Fig. 4i, j, Supplementary Fig. 5d). The substitution also greatly reduced the association of FOXF1 with the HSV-1 promoters (Fig. 4k). Therefore, non-specific DNA backbone interactions, mediated by the conserved tryptophan, are critical for HSV-1 regulation by FOX proteins.

FOXF1 can activate HSV-1 genes and modulate HSV-1 chromatin globally at early times post-infection
We next investigated which viral genes were regulated by FOX proteins and at what stage. At both 3 and 6 hpi with ICP0-null HSV-1, transfected FOXF1 and FOXK1 did not affect viral DNA levels (Fig. 5a), but significantly increased and decreased, respectively, ICP27 (IE gene), TK (E gene) and gC (L gene) mRNA levels regardless of the presence of ACV (Fig. 5b) demonstrating that FOX proteins regulate viral gene transcription at an early stage independent of DNA synthesis.

Regulation of gene transcription is often related to chromatin remodeling. Therefore, we analyzed the association of viral DNA with histone H3 and its modifications by ChIP-qPCR. The occupancies of repressive H3K9me3 and activating H3K18ac and H3K27ac were normalized to those of H3 to assess the fractions of H3 that were modified. Both motif− and motif+ sites were examined. At 2 hpi in N2AFOXF1 cells, DOX-induced FOXF1 expression already significantly decreased total H3 on most sites (Supplementary Fig. 6a, left panel) and decreased H3K9me3/H3 on the ICP8 site while increasing H3K18ac/H3 and H3K27ac/H3 on the ICP27 and UL22 sites (Supplementary Fig. 6a, other panels). At 5 hpi, FOXF1 decreased total H3 on all sites (Fig. 5c, left panel) and H3K9me3/H3 on most sites but increased H3K18ac/H3 and H3K27ac/H3 on all sites (Fig. 5c, other panels). We also analyzed host FOXF1 target sites in Fos and Etv1 genes identified in our ChIP-seq data. Although FOXF1 did not reduce H3 or H3K9me3/H3 on these sites, it did increase H3K18ac/H3 and H3K27ac/H3 on the Etv1 site, and possibly on the Fos site (a trend without significance) (Supplementary Fig. 6b) suggesting that inducing histone acetylation maybe a FOXF1 function applicable to both viral and host genes. We then tested the effects on the viral chromatin further by transfection in Neuro-2a cells and observed decreases in total H3 but increases in H3K27ac/H3 on all the viral sites tested induced by transfected FOXF1 relative to both the empty vector and an irrelevant FOX protein, FOXP1 (Fig. 5d).

The above results strongly indicate that, starting very early during infection, FOXF1 could induce the removal of H3 and H3K9me3 from HSV-1 chromatin while promoting acetylation of the remaining H3. Since all these effects are consistent with chromatin opening, we then performed assays for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC-seq). At 3 h after ICP0-null virus infection of Neuro-2a cells, transfected FOXF1 increased viral reads relative to total reads associated with accessible chromatin (Fig. 5e), and increased accessibility in all viral promoter regions (Fig. 5f). However, signals were increased globally (Supplementary Fig. 6c) along the viral genome without specific peaks like those in the ChIP-seq data suggesting that even though DNA association is partially sequence-specific, the effects on accessibility are non-specific and global.

Such effects made us wonder whether PML-NBs that colocalize with the HSV-1 genome might be affected. Indeed, while basically all control cells showed clear ATRX puncta representing PML-NBs, overexpressed FOXF1 but not FOXK1 caused almost total dispersal of the puncta in ICP0-null virus infected Neuro-2a cells (Fig. 5g). Although these results may be an artifact of FOXF1 overexpression, we note that because PML-NBs contain multiple repressive chromatin remodelers, such as ATRX and DAXX, dispersal of PML-NBs is also in line with activation of viral chromatin.

Activating FOX proteins generally associate with CBP/P300
To understand how FOX proteins modulate viral chromatin, we first considered the observation that FOXA1 binds core histones. Therefore, we pulled down transfected FOXA1, C1, E1, F1 and K1 after Benzonase treatment to digest DNA (Supplementary Fig. 7a) and observed co-immunoprecipitation of histone H3 with all of them (Supplementary Fig. 7b). An H3 antibody also immunoprecipitated transfected FOXF1 (Supplementary Fig. 7c). The association with FOXF1 depended on aa200–380 but not the DBD (Supplementary Fig. 7d) consistent with the observation that FOXA1 uses a non-DBD domain to interact with H3. However, since both activating and repressive FOX proteins associate with H3, this association cannot explain the activating or repressive activities.

To explore binding partners involved in the regulatory activities, we conducted proximity-labeling using FOX proteins fused to TurboID to label proximal proteins by biotin (Fig. 6a, Supplementary Fig. 8a), which were pulled down using streptavidin beads and analyzed by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). FOXF1-TurboID were compared with three negative controls, FOXK1-TurboID, FOXF1Δ200–380-TurboID, and unfused TurboID. Immunofluorescence assays demonstrated nuclear localization of all TurboID-FOX fusion proteins (Supplementary Fig. 8b). After transfection and infection of Neuro-2a cells, comparisons with the three controls commonly identified 53 potential interactors (Fig. 6b, Supplementary Fig. 8c). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database analysis shows that these proteins are predominantly related to ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling (Supplementary Fig. 8d). Application of a more stringent threshold resulted in 11 proteins (Fig. 6b), which form an interaction network according to the STRING database (Supplementary Fig. 8e). Interestingly, homologous histone acetyltransferases CBP and P300, known to stimulate gene transcription by histone acetylation, were both among these 11 proteins. Therefore, we tested their association with FOX proteins further. After Benzonase treatment, co-transfected FOXF1-HA and CBP-Flag were both co-immunoprecipitated by HA and Flag antibodies (Fig. 6c). Immunoprecipitation of transfected FOXF1 pulled down endogenous CBP, too (Fig. 6d). Transfected CBP also co-immunoprecipitated with transfected FOXA1, C1 and E1, but not with FOXK1 or FOXF1Δ200–300 (Fig. 6e, Supplementary Fig. 9). Therefore, activating but not repressive FOX proteins generally associate with CBP/P300.

FOXF1 recruits CBP/P300 to acetylate histones in HSV-1 chromatin and stimulate viral gene transcription
Next, we examined the effects of these FOXF1 proximal proteins. We knocked down each of these except TTN, which is not implicated in gene regulation (NCBI database), and found that siRNAs that effectively knocked down BCL9L, CREBBP (CBP), EP300 (P300) or ARID1A (Supplementary Table 1) decreased viral yields in FOXF1 overexpressing cells, and a second set of siRNAs confirmed the effects of CBP, P300 and ARID1A but not BCL9L (Fig. 6f). We then focused on CBP/P300. Surprisingly, in the absence of FOXF1, both dual knockdown of CBP and P300 and a specific CBP/P300 inhibitor (A-485) substantially increased yields of both ICP0-null and WT HSV-1 at 48 hpi indicating that CBP/P300 normally suppresses HSV-1 replication perhaps indirectly (Fig. 6g, h, Supplementary Fig. 10a, b), such that the differences between viral yields in the presence and absence of FOXF1 were eliminated or greatly reduced. This suggests that FOXF1 requires CBP/P300 to efficiently activate HSV-1 replication. Even at 3 hpi, the dual knockdown greatly attenuated the stimulation of viral gene expression by FOXF1 (Supplementary Fig. 10c) suggesting that CBP/P300 acts at the early stage of transcription.

To test whether CBP/P300 mediates stimulation of viral chromatin acetylation by FOXF1 (Fig. 5c), we used A-485 in ChIP-qPCR assays. At 5 hpi, in the absence of FOXF1, A-485 had little effect on the baseline H3K27ac/H3 levels on the viral sites (Fig. 6i) and even increased H3K18ac/H3 on some sites (Supplementary Fig. 10d) suggesting that CBP/P300 does not acetylate HSV-1 chromatin without FOXF1. Remarkably, in the presence of FOXF1, A-485 significantly reduced H3K27ac/H3 on all viral sites tested, with stronger impacts on motif+ than motif− sites. A-485 also decreased H3K18ac/H3 on the motif+ but not motif− sites. Regardless, the increases in histone acetylation on viral sites caused by FOXF1 were largely eliminated by A-485 for both modifications, which strongly suggests that FOXF1 recruits CBP/P300 to acetylate histones associated with the HSV-1 genome.

FOXK1 associates with SIN3A and MAX to repress HSV-1 replication and antagonizes activating FOX proteins
To understand the repressive mechanisms of FOXK1, we re-used the proteomic data to identify proteins proximal to FOXK1-TurboID relative to FOXF1-TurboID and unfused TurboID, resulting in 85 proteins (Fig. 7a), among which MAX, KIN, GTF2A1, SIN3A and ARID4B are implicated in gene regulation (NCBI database). Among siRNAs for these genes, each of two siRNAs against MAX and one of two siRNAs against SIN3A increased ICP0-null HSV-1 yields in Neuro-2a cells overexpressing FOXK1 (Supplementary Table 1, Fig. 7b, Supplementary Fig. 11a). In FOXK1 KO cells, both SIN3A siRNAs eliminated virus suppression by transfected FOXK1 and both MAX siRNAs attenuated the suppression (Fig. 7c) suggesting that FOXK1 work with MAX and SIN3A to suppress HSV-1 replication. Because SIN3A is a scaffolding protein known to recruit histone deacetylases to chromatin, we further investigated the role of histone deacetylation. Interestingly, treatment with a histone deacetylase inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA), a chemical that can induce reactivation in neuronal culture models, not only increased viral yields substantially, but also weakened the suppressive effects of FOXK1 (Fig. 7d) suggesting that histone deacetylation is involved in FOXK1 function. Since the effects of MAX siRNAs were remarkably substantial, we also tried single guide RNAs (sgRNAs). All three sgRNAs effectively reduced MAX expression (Supplementary Fig. 11b) and caused ~2-log increases in viral yields (Fig. 7e), which further indicates that MAX strongly suppresses HSV-1 replication. Although we failed to co-immunoprecipitate FOXK1 with MAX or SIN3A (Supplementary Fig. 9), Western blotting of biotin-captured FOXK1 proximal proteins labeled using FOXK1-TurboID readily detected MAX and SIN3A (Fig. 7f) confirming their proximity to FOXK1. We note that previous studies reported FOXK1-SIN3A interactions in yeast two-hybrid and co-immunoprecipitation assays. It is possible that these protein-protein interactions are transient, weak and/or indirect, so that they did not persist during our co-immunoprecipitation assay.

Given that FOXF1 associates with co-activators while FOXK1 is at least proximal to co-repressors and may function with them to repress HSV-1 replication, we wondered whether activating and repressive FOX proteins are antagonistic. Indeed, during co-transfection, FOXK1 abolished the strong effects of simultaneously expressed FOXA1 and E1, and greatly reduced the effects of FOXC1 and F1 on ICP0-null HSV-1 replication (Fig. 7g). Antagonism of FOXA1 was also achieved by FOXK2, but not by FOXP1, FOXH1, or the DBDs of FOXC1 or A1 (Fig. 7h) suggesting that non-DBD domains are required for the antagonism. Therefore, FOXK proteins work with repressive cofactors to antagonize activating FOX proteins.
