### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors investigate the role of FOX family transcription factors in regulating the lytic-latent balance of herpesviruses, with the primary focus on herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). The study identifies specific activating (FOX A, C, E, and F family members) and repressive (FOX K1 and K2) FOX proteins and investigates their mechanisms of action through a range of sequencing and molecular assays. While the majority of the work is in mouse cells, some of the activity could be recapitulated in human cells to varying degrees between cell lines, indicating a general but cell type-dependent effect. RNA-seq indicates that repressive FOXK proteins are widely expressed while the activating proteins are more abundant in non-neuronal cells, but expression of activating FOX proteins increases in neurons after infection or cellular stress. Focusing on latency, reducing the basal levels of repressive FOXK1 and 2 in trigeminal ganglia of infected mice with siRNAs was sufficient to induce reactivation along transduction of activating FOX proteins. Furthermore, FOX proteins were found to bind the viral genome extensively, even at sites lacking the RAAACA motif seen for host genes. The functional activating/repressive activity was found through screening of FOX mutants to depend on backbone interactions rather than the recognition of this motif. Using timepoints and chemical inhibitors of viral DNA replication, the role of FOX proteins was shown to occur early in the viral lifecycle. Interestingly, expression of FOXF1 even dispersed silencing PML bodies, mimicking one of the major roles of the viral ICP0 protein. Through a series of IP assays and proximity labeling assays, the authors identify activating FOX proteins interacting with chromatin remodelers, namely CBP/P300, and that this leads to increased H3 acetylation and opening of viral chromatin. On the other hand, repressive FOXK1 interacts with MAX and SIN3A to provide the repressive role through the opposite effect.
Overall, the manuscript provides a thorough investigation of FOX proteins and their roles in viral replication through of a number of techniques and settings. It links binding of these proteins to the viral genome to functional roles in chromatin formation of viral DNA and outcomes on viral gene expression and titers, however it would be helpful to have the ChIP and ATAC-Seq done on latently infected neurons before and after induction of FOX members. The techniques are well described and the findings presented well, and the findings should be on interest to researchers investigating neurotrophic DNA viruses. I have a few comments for consideration:
Major Comments
Some clarification on the design of the siRNAs used for knockdown experiments is required, or more direct evidence of their functionality such as Westerns when antibodies are available. According to Table S1, the siRNA sequences are perfectly complementary and lack the two-nucleotide 3' overhangs essential for loading into the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).
The authors indicate that BoHV-1 inefficiently infects N2A neurons, and use an MOI of 5 MDBK units. Could the authors provide a relative MOI for N2A cells based on TCID50 assays and immunofluorescence?
Regarding FOX ChIP-Seq peaks around transcription start sites, could this analysis be extended to metagene analyses of host and viral genes? On this note, does the RTAAACA motif exist in other parts of the viral genome that did not give rise to peaks in ChIP?
Without a marker for infection, it is difficult to claim that the cells in Fig. S6B are both infected and transfected. There is only one cell, in the FOXF1+WT HSV panel at the bottom right, that shows a dispersal of DAPI signal due to viral replication compartments.
Minor Comments
Line 40: change to "an ubiquitous"
Perhaps the authors could elaborate more on the HSV1FOXC1 virus mutants so readers get an overview without having to reference the earlier study
Line 443: perhaps the authors mean PLO, which is a more common abbreviation for poly-L-ornithine
Line 649: place a space in the middle of "pH8.0" for consistency
The supplemental figures do not need "supplemental data" in the title
The ChIP and ATAC-seq are already publicly available, but I was unable to locate the proteomics data with the given accession number

### Reviewer 3

In their manuscript, Xiang et al. investigate the role of FOX proteins — a family of transcription factors – in HSV-1 replication. The authors use a variety of approaches and sophisticated methods to decipher the functions of FOX proteins in controlling HSV-1 latency, including proximity labelling experiments to identify potential FOXF1- and FOXK1-interacting proteins with roles in gene regulation.
At the editor’s request, this review focuses exclusively on the proteomic experiments presented in the manuscript. Overall, the proteomic studies are well designed, appear to have been conducted by experienced proteomics researchers, and are analysed using appropriate cut-off criteria. Please see my specific comments below.
Major comments
1. The authors state that their proteomic data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange repository under the dataset identifier PXD059232, and that the dataset should be publicly available. However, I was unable to locate the dataset using this identifier, or by searching relevant keywords or author names. I urge the authors to verify the accuracy of the dataset ID and ensure that the data are publicly accessible at the time of review. If the dataset is still private, reviewer credentials should be provided to allow proper evaluation of the proteomic data.
Minor comments
1. I commend the authors for clearly distinguishing between proteins that are proximal to the bait protein and those that directly interact with it — a distinction that is often overlooked in proximity labelling studies and in many manuscripts I have reviewed previously.
2. The authors should provide more detailed information on how the proteomic data were processed, including steps such as the handling of missing values, removal of potential contaminants, normalization procedures, and any filtering criteria applied. Additionally, specify which software tools or statistical packages were used for the analysis.
3. The authors may consider validating the nuclear localisation of the TurboID-tagged FOX constructs using IF to confirm their proper subcellular distribution, and include these data in Fig. S8.
4. Fig. 6: It would be helpful to include a Venn diagram in to highlight the 11 proteins enriched by more than 2 log2 in all pairwise comparisons. This addition would improve the overall flow of the figure and help readers more easily understand the rationale behind validating the interaction with CBP in panels C–E, as well as the selection of genes shown in panel F for silencing experiments.
5. Fig. 7A: Would MAX, KIN, GTF2A1, SIN3A, and ARID4B still be considered hits if a more stringent cut-off of log₂ fold-change > 2 were applied, as was done for the FOXF1 dataset? This may be particularly relevant given that MAX and SIN3A were not successfully validated in the co-IP assays, which—beyond the possibility of a temporal or indirect interaction, as the authors suggest—could also indicate that the interactions are generally weaker. Along these lines, were the authors able to validate, via co-IP, the interaction between FOXK1 and any other protein that showed a similar level of enrichment as MAX or SIN3A? Generally, increasing the amount of protein input in co-IP assays can improve the likelihood of successful detection, which might be worth considering if validation has been challenging.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We thank the reviewers for taking time to review this manuscript and providing many helpful comments. We have addressed all points raised by the reviewers and included new data from the requested experiments. We believe that these revisions have greatly improved the manuscript. The point-by-point responses are written under the corresponding comments in bold letters.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript “Counteracting FOX proteins epigenetically control the herpesvirus lytic-latent balance” by Xiang et al. describes the role of FOX pioneer transcription factors in HSV-1 replication. The family of FOX transcription factors consists of several members in humans that are known for their role in embryonic development. FOX proteins consist of a forkhead box (winged helix) that mediates binding to DNA. The authors convincingly show that some family members have either an antiviral or proviral role in HSV-1 replication, which is an important finding per se. The manuscript is well-written and well-structured in general. There are too many jumps from one FOX protein to another between the individual images which is somehow confusing. In my opinion, the manuscript would have benefited from focusing on maybe two FOX proteins, one promoting viral replication and one hampering viral replication. The data about how FOX proteins influence viral replication in vitro and in vivo are convincing. However, the mechanistic studies would benefit from additional experiments, in particular in regard to ChIP / ChIP-seq. experiments. Most experiments were performed with overexpressed proteins, which is not the best setting to study transcription factor binding to DNA.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive comments as well as the constructive suggestions for improvement. Regarding the comments regarding the jumps from one FOX protein to another, we apologize for the confusion. Focusing on two FOX proteins, FOXF1 and FOXK1, was mainly what we did in mechanistic studies. Some results about other FOX proteins were included only for confirmation. To clarify, we have added this sentence at the beginning of mechanistic investigation: “The following studies focused mainly on FOXF1 and FOXK1 as examples of an activator and repressor, respectively, of viral replication and reactivation.” We have also added the names of the FOX proteins on some figure panels with indications regarding whether they are activating or repressive in some places. Regarding the additional experiments, we agree that overexpressed proteins can sometimes be problematic and address this issue below under the relevant major points.
Major points:
- Throughout the manuscript the authors use a ICP0-null HSV-1 virus based on an initial experiment in Figure 1 where they show that both ICP0-null virus and wildtype virus behave similar. However, it would be crucial to repeat some of the key experiments also with a wildtype virus to exclude effects that are due to the absence of ICP0.
Response: We understand the concern. Our rationale for using an ICP0-null virus was that FOX proteins have greater effects on it than on wild-type (WT) virus suggesting that ICP0 interferes with FOX protein functions, making it harder to dissect the mechanisms. We note that in our original submission most of our functional studies were conducted using WT virus (Figs 1-3), and that absence of ICP0 is biologically relevant during latency and the initial stages of reactivation. Nevertheless, we repeated experiments regarding the effects of knocking down CBP/P300 on FOXF1 functions with WT virus and have added the results in Fig. S10B. Moreover, the new ChIP experiments in 293T cells (see below and Fig. 4A) were also conducted using both WT and ICP0-null viruses.
- Along this line, ICP0 is a ubiquitin E3-ligase. Could the authors please show a western blot +/- infection with wt / delta ICP0 virus in cells that have endogenous expression of most of the FOX proteins (e.g. BJ fibroblasts and HepG2). This would show how virus infection affects physiological FOX protein levels and whether ICP0 is able to degrade some of the FOX proteins.
Response: We have done this in 293T cells, which have substantial endogenous expression of most of the FOX proteins we have studied. The results have been added to Fig. S1B. The FOX protein levels were largely unaffected by ICP0. We speculate that ICP0 interference with FOX protein functions may be related to the ability of both ICP0 and FOX proteins to regulate viral chromatin.
- The finding that FOXF1 is supposed to have a different binding motive in the viral genome compared to the host genome is quite unusual. In general, I am critical of ChIP assays in the context of protein overexpression because overexpression often leads to artifacts. Transcription factors possess the ability to bind to DNA and the more transcription factor present, the more binding to DNA. The authors should perform ChIP assays in infected cells (HSV-1 wt / delta ICP0) with endogenous FOXF1 expression with antibody Abcam; ab168383 from Cancer Discov (2018) 8 (2): 234–251. https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-17-0468.
Response: We do not think our data suggest that FOXF1 has different binding motifs in the viral genome relative to the host genome and we did not state that. The two de novo motifs in Fig. 4C look similar and both conform to the RTAAACA consensus sequence. The minor difference may be because the viral genome is too small to allow accurate motif determination. We share the reviewer’s concerns about experiments using overexpression. Our original thought was to study this in neuronal cells where FOXF1 is poorly expressed so we used overexpression to mimic the condition where FOXF1 expression is induced due to stresses. We thank the reviewer for providing information about the antibody. We have used the antibody for ChIP-qPCR in 293T cells and have demonstrated FOXF1 association with all the viral sites as well as two host sites tested. Two of the viral sites tested (in UL22 and UL50 genes) conform to the motifs in Fig. 4C and two of the viral sites (in ICP8 and ICP27 promoters) do not conform to it supporting our finding that FOXF1 associates with viral DNA in both sequence-specific and nonspecific manners. These new data are in Fig. 4A. This indeed strengthens the argument that FOXF1 can associate with viral DNA broadly in physiological conditions.
- In addition, the authors must include a suitable transfection control protein in their ChIP-seq. assay and ChIP assays in Figure 4 and 6. Desirable would be to use another FOX transcription factor from Figure 1 that did not affect HSV-1 replication like FOXO1.
Response: Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we used FOXP1 (for which we found a good commercially available antibody) as a transfection control for the added experiment of FOXF1 ChIP in 293T cells (Fig. 4A). However, we detected FOXP1 association with both the host and viral DNA sites (FOXF1 association is still higher than FOXP1, but they are both much higher than the IgG negative control). This is not surprising because FOX proteins have similar binding motifs. This raises the interesting possibility that FOX proteins generally associate with the viral genome but such association is insufficient to confer regulation of viral genes.
With regard to Fig. 6I, it was performed using a cell line with inducible FOXF1 expression, not by transfection. Nevertheless, we added an experiment which examined the effects of transfected FOXF1 on H3K27ac/H3, where both transfected FOXP1 and the empty vector were used as negative controls (Fig. 5D, right panel). The results recapitulated the results using inducible cell lines (Fig. 5C) and also showed similar H3K27ac/H3 values between FOXP1 and the empty vector-transfected cells suggesting that the results in Fig. 6I from inducible cell lines should be valid.
- The authors should also show selected regions from the host genome in order to compare FOXF1 binding to the human genome upon FOXF1 overexpression with more physiological settings e.g. from Cancer Discov (2018) 8 (2): 234–251. A list with all binding sites in the host and viral genomes in the supplement would also help.
Response: The positions of viral and host peaks and their corresponding genes are listed in Supplementary Data File 1. For host sites, since they are too numerous, we selected the top 1000. Among them are many binding sites in the mouse genome reported previously (Data source: Cistrome Data Browser, GSM2062274), such as Sfi1, Bcl10, Mpzl1, Fos, Tex14, Ablim1, Fcho2, Ints3, Pitpnc1, Ncor2, etc. The experiments in the recommended Cancer Discov article used human cells, but we used mouse cells, so the sequences are not directly comparable. Nevertheless, we detected peaks on Etv1 and Gpr20 genes, which were identified as FOXF1 targets also in the published study.
- For Figure 5C, does FOXF1 expression also induce changes in Histone H3 / Histone modifications at binding sites in cellular chromatin?
Response: We analyzed sites in cellular Fos and Etv1 genes, which are high-ranking host sites in our ChIP-seq data. We see that on the Etv1 site, both H3K18ac/H3 and H3K27ac/H3 ratios were increased by induced FOXF1 expression, with the same trend observed with the Fos site. However, H3 and H3K9me3/H3 on these sites were not reduced like the viral sites. We conclude that inducing histone acetylation may be a FOXF1 function applicable to both viral and host genes. The added data are in Fig. S6B.
- The authors show dispersal of PML-nuclear bodies by FOXF1. That would mean that cell lines like HeLa, 293T and BJ fibroblasts that express FOXF1 (Fig. 2A) should not have PML bodies, which is obviously not the case. In addition, ICP0 is highly efficient in degrading PML-nuclear bodies. This would mean that disruption of PML bodies by FOXF1 has no physiological relevance in the context of wildtype infections because it is anyway rapidly degraded upon infection. Could the authors please comment.
Response: The reviewer’s argument about the PML-NB makes sense, but the argument about ICP0 makes sense only with regard to acute infection. During latent infection as well as the initial stage of reactivation, there is little or no ICP0 expression, so FOXF1 can regulate PML bodies in these stages of infection. Regardless, we admit that it is possible that we introduced FOXF1 to levels that were artificially high. Therefore, we downplay this part by deleting the corresponding supplemental data. We have kept the panel in the main text because we still think FOXF1 dispersal of PML bodies is an interesting phenomenon that deserves revealing, and it may be physiologically relevant under stress conditions where certain Fox genes are strongly induced according to our data in Fig. 2. We also added the following sentence as a caution in the text: “Although these results may be an artifact of FOXF1 overexpression, we note that…”.
- Minor point:
The study would benefit from IF experiments analyzing the presence of FOX proteins in viral replication compartments e.g. by co-staining with ICP8.
Response: This has been done and we see partial colocalization. The additional results are in Fig. S4A. We used an ICP4 antibody to stain replication compartments, which in our hands works well.
- In some experiments (e.g. in Figures 4 F,H,I,J) the authors used a low MOI of 0.2 and virus was titrated after 48h. Would the effect be the same with higher MOI of 1 after 24h?
Response: We understand the reason to check effects at higher MOIs and shorter times. We did the experiment using the W122A mutants as a representative (see below). The result is the same as MOI of 0.2 and 48 h. We believe the other mutants also behave similar between the two conditions. We do not see a need to put this in the manuscript given the already crowded figures.
